KEYWORDS Brownian motion, extinction and persistence, hantavirus, human spillover infection, numerical simulation, public health risk, rodent-borne transmission, sir–sir model 1 Introduction According to the latest WHO update on 12 May 2026, a multi- country hantavirus cluster linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship reported 11 cases, including three deaths. Among these cases, nine were confirmed as Andes virus infections and two were classified as probable cases. WHO noted that all reported cases occurred among passengers or crew members, and no additional deaths had been reported since WHO was first informed of the cluster on 2 May 2026 (1). Hantavirus remains an important emerging zoonotic pathogen, reflecting the breadth of its reservoir, severity of clinical manifestations and ongoing public health importance, as evidenced by recent literature. D’Souza and Patel surveyed hantaviruses of the New World and their relevance to biodefense and viewed them as serious diseases potentially from a natural source in rodents, but are difficult to cultivate and disseminate in practice (2). Likewise, in Canada, Warner et al. investigated hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and found that the deer mouse was the primary reservoir host, and Sin Nombre virus was the leading cause of human disease (3). The authors also mentioned that rodent exposure, environmental modification, and poor surveillance are significant risk factors for zoonotic spillover of hantavirus and discussed the issue in the wider context of zoonotic spillover in general (4). Recent research has enhanced understanding of the molecular and virological mechanisms of hantavirus replication, structure, and immune evasion. Meier et al. gave an updated structural virology review of the hantavirus replication cycle, elucidating the mechanisms of viral entry, genome replication, assembly, and release, as well as how these mechanisms relate to antiviral and vaccine development targets (5). Zhang et al. explained the ability of hantaviruses to disrupt innate antiviral signaling, which contributes to the ability to persistently infect reservoir hosts that are typically healthy and to cause severe disease in humans (6). Engdahl et al. also made a contribution to this field, by mapping human antibody responses against hantavirus antigens, which can aid in vaccine development and serological diagnostics (7). Studies conducted during this period include transmission and outbreak studies and underscore the ongoing need for surveillance and early detection. Toledo et al. conducted a systematic review of the evidence and found that Andes virus might be transmitted from person-to- person, but more controlled studies are needed (8). Sah et al. reviewed recent hantavirus outbreaks and pointed out that there are still no specific approved treatments, high fatality risks, and delayed diagnosis of hantavirus, which are still major clinical challenges (9). Goodfellow et al. described an infection with an orthohantavirus in humans in Michigan, USA, indicating that physicians should be aware of the possibility of a hantavirus infection beyond the classic “hotspot” areas where exposure to hantaviruses is known to occur and when signs and symptoms are consistent with exposure history. During this time, too, there has been a growth of clinical literature (10). Afzal et al. examined the available therapeutic options such as antiviral agents, immune-based treatments, and vaccine candidates, but found that supportive care is the primary management approach due to the lack of a widely accepted targeted therapy for hantavirus (11). Vial et al. summarized clinical features, diagnosis, management, and prevention of hantavirus infection in humans, describing the disease as a zoonotic viral haemorrhagic infection with significant clinical relevance, an emerging disease (12). Wu et al. emphasized the importance of hantavirus in children with acute kidney injury and thrombocytopenia, suggesting that hantavirus should be included in the differential diagnosis of pediatric acute kidney injury patients with thrombocytopenia (13). Hantavirus distribution in the region/ecology is influenced by reservoir ecology, geography, land use and human exposure. Chen et al. reviewed zoonotic members of the family Hantaviridae of global health importance and highlighted the importance of integrated ecological, molecular and epidemiological surveillance (14). Lupusoru et al. summarized the situation with hantavirus infections in South-Eastern Europe, particularly in relation to Puumala and Dobrava viruses, and associated the distribution of reservoirs with the patterns of disease in the region (15). Mello et al. studied the expansion of hantavirus within natural host populations and linked the ecological changes, host distribution, and spillover risk (16). These population level and seroepidemiological studies also show that exposure to hantavirus is not uniform among regions or occupational groups. Whitmer et al. investigated the prevalence and genotype distribution of human orthohantavirus disease in the United States, identifying regional clustering and gaps that affect case detection (17). Tortosa et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of hantavirus seroprevalence in non-epidemic settings and revealed that exposures vary by geography, occupation and study population (18). Gubareva et al. studied the prevalence of hantavirus antibodies in high-risk adults in Western Kazakhstan and determined occupational and environmental exposures that potentially could be factors in hantavirus infection (19). Studies of hantavirus reservoirs and wildlife have recently documented the continued importance of animal surveillance for preventing hantavirus. Goodfellow et al. studied the circulation and shedding of human-pathogenic hantaviruses in various rodent reservoirs, which helped their study to clarify the environmental exposure risk for hantaviruses in infected hosts (20). Guo et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of hantaviruses in small mammals of Southeast Asia, and recommended for expanding the surveillance of wildlife for the detection of zoonotic risk in advance (21). Stochastic delay modeling provides a framework for describing real-world systems affected by both random environmental Frontiers in Public Health 02 frontiersin.org Raza et al. 10.3389/fpubh.2026.1880617 variations and delayed responses. By including uncertainty and time-lag terms in the mathematical model, it reflects system behavior more accurately. This approach helps improve prediction and gives deeper insight into complex dynamic processes. The paper is organized as follows. Section 1 presents the introduction and background of the study. Section 2 describes the preliminary concepts from stochastic analysis and stochastic delay differential equations. Section 3 formulates the stochastic delay hantavirus model using susceptible, infected, and recovered human populations together with susceptible, infected, and recovered rodent populations. Section 4 discusses the qualitative analysis, including positivity, boundedness, disease-free and endemic equilibria, reproduction numbers, extinction, and persistence. Section 5 presents the real reported hantavirus data and its connection with the model. Section 6 introduces the numerical schemes, including Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and stochastic NSFD methods. Section 7 provides graphical simulations and interpretation of the numerical results. Finally, Section 8 gives the concluding remarks and possible future extensions. 2 Preliminaries In this section, we recall some basic concepts from stochastic analysis and stochastic delay differential equations that are used in the formulation and qualitative analysis of the stochastic delay hantavirus model. Definition 1 (Brownian motion (22, 23)). A real-valued stochastic process {W(t), t ≥0} defined on a complete probability space (, F, P) is called a standard Brownian motion if it satisfies the following properties: 1. W(0) = 0 almost surely; 2. W(t) −W(s) is independent of Fs for all 0 ≤s < t; 3. W(t) −W(s) ∼N(0, t −s) for all 0 ≤s < t; 4. W(t) has continuous sample paths almost surely. Definition 2 (Stochastic delay differential equation (23)). A stochastic delay differential equation is an equation in which the present rate of change of a stochastic process depends on both its current state and its past state. A general SDDE can be written as dX(t) = f  t, X(t), X(t −τ)  dt + g  t, X(t), X(t −τ)  dW(t), where τ > 0 is a fixed delay, f is the drift coefficient, g is the diffusion coefficient, and W(t) is a standard Brownian motion. Definition 3 (Initial history function (23)). For an SDDE with delay τ > 0, the solution is determined not only by the value at t = 0 but also by its past values on the interval [−τ, 0]. Thus, the initial condition is prescribed as a continuous history function X(θ) = φ(θ), θ ∈[−τ, 0], where φ ∈C([−τ, 0], Rn +). Here, C([−τ, 0], Rn +) denotes the space of continuous functions from [−τ, 0] into Rn +. Definition 4 (Positive solution (22, 23)). A solution X(t) of an SDDE is said to be positive if X(t) > 0 almost surely for all t ≥0, whenever the initial history satisfies X(θ) = φ(θ) > 0, θ ∈[−τ, 0]. In biological models, positivity ensures that population variables remain meaningful. Definition 5 (Mean-square stability (23)). The disease-free state is said to be mean-square stable with respect to an infected compartment I(t) if lim t→∞E  I2(t)  = 0. If, in addition, there exist constants K > 0 and λ > 0 such that E  I2(t)  ≤Ke−λt, then the disease-free state is said to be exponentially stable in the mean-square sense. Definition 6 (Non-negative solution (22, 23)). A solution X(t) of an SDDE is said to be non-negative if X(t) ∈Rn + almost surely for all t ≥0, whenever the initial history satisfies X(θ) = φ(θ) ∈Rn +, θ ∈[−τ, 0]. In biological models, non-negativity ensures that population variables remain meaningful. 3 Model formulation Following the deterministic hantavirus transmission structure between humans and rodents, we divide the human population into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes, denoted by SH(t), IH(t), and RH(t), respectively. Similarly, the rodent population is divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes, denoted by SR(t), IR(t), and RR(t), respectively. Thus, NH(t) = SH(t) + IH(t) + RH(t), NR(t) = SR(t) + IR(t) + RR(t). The deterministic model assumes that hantavirus is transmitted from infected rodents to susceptible humans and among rodents, while human-to-human and human-to-rodent transmission are neglected. To make the model more realistic, we extend the system by including random environmental fluctuations, incubation or response delays, and exponential survival effects during the delay period. analysis.methods: An SIR–SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations was formulated, then extended with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays and exponential delay‑survival effects, and numerical simulations were performed using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta and stochastic nonstandard finite‑difference (SNSFD) methods.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease with human infection occurring via spillover from rodent reservoirs, posing ongoing public‑health concerns. Methods: The authors formulated an SIR–SIR transmission model for interacting rodent and human populations, extended it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete delays and exponential delay‑survival effects, and performed numerical simulations using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta and stochastic nonstandard finite‑difference methods. Results: Analysis indicated that virus persistence is driven mainly by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human cases arise from spillover, and that stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote extinction. Contribution: The study provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic stochastic delay framework for hantavirus risk assessment and highlights that controlling infection in rodent reservoirs is the most effective way to reduce persistence and human spillover; it also demonstrates superior stability of the SNSFD scheme for such simulations. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 使用随机延迟模型对欧洲鼠源性 汉坦病毒 溢出进行公共卫生风险评估

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是一种啮齿动物传播的人畜共患疾病,啮齿动物为主要储存宿主,人类通过溢出暴露获得感染,构成持续的公共卫生关注。
analysis_zh.methods: 构建了一个用于相互作用的啮齿动物和人类种群的SIR–SIR传播框架,随后加入布朗随机扰动、离散时间延迟和指数延迟存活效应,并使用Euler–Maruyama、随机Runge–Kutta以及随机非标准有限差分(SNSFD)方法进行数值模拟。
analysis_zh.results: 分析表明,汉坦病毒的持续主要由啮齿动物间传播驱动,而人类感染来源于溢出;在特定条件下,随机扰动和延迟存活效应可降低有效再生阈值并促进疾病消亡。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文提供了一个数学严谨、符合生物实际的随机延迟模型用于汉坦病毒风险评估,强调控制啮齿动物储存宿主内的感染是降低持续性和人类溢出的最有效策略,并展示了SNSFD方案在此类模拟中的卓越数值稳定性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Hantavirus: A Zoonotic Pathogen and Its Role in Achieving Sustainable Development
papers.abstract: Zoonoses meaning the transmission of infections between animals and humans, remain a challenge for human and veterinary health institutions worldwide. Despite advancements in various medical fields, there are still failures in eradicating zoonotic pathogens and preventing their recurring outbreaks, especially viral ones. Among these zoonotic virus is Hantavirus (single-stranded RNA), that emergence has caused panic and fears due to its high mortality rate. The infection is primarily transmitted to humans through rodents such as mice, causing serious illnesses such as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. Therefore, reviewing basic information about this infection, the role of environmental factors, and modes of transmission is crucial for prevention, enabling to avoid infection and mitigate human, animal, and economic losses. One of the most important strategies for infection control is the implementation of the One Health approach, which closely integrates human, animal, and environmental health—the golden triad—and is linked to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This approach aims for comprehensive improvements in the environment, veterinary care, and human well-being.
papers.journal: International Journal of Multidisciplinary and Innovative Research

Despite advancements in various medical fields, there are still failures in eradicating zoonotic pathogens and preventing their recurring outbreaks, especially viral ones. Among these zoonotic virus is Hantavirus (single-stranded RNA), that emergence has caused panic and fears due to its high mortality rate. The infection is primarily transmitted to humans through rodents such as mice, causing serious illnesses such as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. Therefore, reviewing basic information about this infection, the role of environmental factors, and modes of transmission is crucial for prevention, enabling to avoid infection and mitigate human, animal, and economic losses. One of the most important strategies for infection control is the implementation of the One Health approach, which closely integrates human, animal, and environmental health—the golden triad—and is linked to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This approach aims for comprehensive improvements in the environment, veterinary care, and human well-being. KEYWORDS: Zoonotic pathogens, Hantavirus, infection, One Health. Published On: 23 July 2026 Available on: https://ijmir.com INTRODUCTION Zoonoses, being always at the interface of human and animal health, remain among the most life-threatening infectious risks and hazards today. Zoonotic infection is thus one of the most important threats to human health and the environment today because it has great impacts on the fate of humans and animals [1-3]. Most human infections are zoonotic, which means that there is a strong association between the animal reservoirs and human infections. This is in line with the World Health Organization which states that about 60% of new infectious diseases are zoonotic, derived from transmission events [4,5]. The continuous polygenic transmission of diseases from animals, directly or indirectly, is an essential element in the establishment of new zoonotic infections and their subsequent transmission to humans [6]. This process is further facilitated by changes in agricultural practices and environmental conditions that bring humans into contact with numerous animal species, expanding the opportunities for inter- species transmission [7]. Zoonoses are a wide variety of infectious agents; viruses, bacteria, parasites, fungi, and even prions that can be transmitted between animals and humans [8,9]. In assessments that highlight increased risks of intensive livestock production and other stressors, we underscore this treatment gap and the need for approaches to disease emergence and the management of therapeutic resources, especially antimicrobials [10]. Environmental interconnectedness has over the years ramped up the risk of zoonotic viral pathogens at a global scale. This, therefore, will require sustained surveillance, knowledge of viral evolution, effective public health response, and proactive prevention to lower infection and fatality rates [11,12]. Hantavirus is one of these viral zoonotic infections; it is a highly pathogenic and transmissible pathogen that relates to human, animal, and environmental health. Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses having a global distribution, wherein pathogenic strains infect several species of rodents [13]. In altered habitats hanta virus is mainly spread by rodents and can lead to severe respiratory and kidney problems in humans. Changes in the environment and in the rodent populations directly influence the risks of human exposure, leading to less predictable patterns of transmission and a closer association with environmental disturbance [14]. Frequently, the mode of transmission is through contact with contaminated rodent saliva, faeces or urine, and perhaps augmented by inhalation of aerosols in places recently occupied by rats or during activities that generate contaminated dust. The principles of hanta virus have a Hantavirus: A Zoonotic Pathogen and Its Role in Achieving Sustainable Development 613 Volume 03 Issue 07 July 2026 Corresponding Author: Ozdan Akram Ghareeb worldwide impact in the general trend of infection risks and the perpetual requirement of surveillance [15,16]. This article reviews basic principles needed to understand and focuses on reservoirs of infection and transmission pathways, assessing risks and applying preventive measures, tying them to the achievement of the Sustainable Development goals. Emergence of Hantavirus Hantavirus is becoming increasingly significant due to various interrelated factors: 1-Climate Change: This upsets ecological equilibrium by compelling rodents to relocate towards human settlements, so facilitating the influx of the virus into their populations. Droughts compel rodents to travel towards human settlements, where the principal reservoir sources sustenance from their populations. This compelled relocation directly affects individuals [17]. 2. Urbanization and Deforestation: The danger of coming into contact with disease vectors from animals has undoubtedly increased with urban sprawl and deforestation [18]. 3- Increased health risks: The high mortality rate, which can reach 40% in some respiratory syndromes, is a serious threat to global health security, particularly in the absence of specialized treatments or approved vaccines [19]. HANTAVIRUS STRUCTURE It belongs to the order Bunyavirales and family Hantaviridae (genus Orthohantavirus), the outline is as follows: - Viral envelope: It is a virus that is being enveloped with a spherical or oval form, with a lipid bilayer derived from the host cell membrane. - Surface Proteins: The envelope carries protruding glycoprotein projections termed Gn and Gc. These enable the virus to bind to host cell receptors and assist in the entry of the virus into the cells [20]. GENETIC MATERIAL (GENOME) The virus has a genome consisting of single-stranded RNA of negative sense as illustrate in figure (1). Genome segments The genome is made up of three major segments, or a tripartite genome: 1- The small segment (S): it houses the information for the nucleocapsid protein that RNA is protected with. 2- The medium segment (M): this segment contains information for the envelope glycoproteins (Gn and Gc). 3- The large segment (L): codes for the viral replication enzyme (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) [21]. Figure 1 : Structure of Hantavirus. VIRUS RESERVOIRS Humans are not a host for the Hantavirus. Instead, the virus is transmitted to humans from specific animal hosts that include: 1-Rodents: These are the primary host and vector and include field mice and rats (such as the deer mouse and the Norway rat). Interestingly, rodents infected with the virus do not show any symptoms but carry and shed it throughout their lives as a chronic infection [22]. 2-Insectivores and Bats: Recent research has shown that some types of shrews, moles and bats also act as [23]. TRANSMISSION TO HUMANS The virus is transmitted to humans in several ways (Figure 2), most notably: 1- Inhalation as the primary route: This is the case when aerosols contaminated with small droplets from the urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents is inhaled. Such aerosols are commonly generated during the cleaning of warehouses, abandoned houses, or fields. Hantavirus: A Zoonotic Pathogen and Its Role in Achieving Sustainable Development 614 Volume 03 Issue 07 July 2026 Corresponding Author: Ozdan Akram Ghareeb 2- Direct contact: This involves touching the hand of a person who has contacted contaminated secretions and then touching one's eyes, nose, or mouth [24]. 3- Bites: This is a direct bite from an infected rodent (a less common route) [25]. 4- Human-to-human transmission: This is very rare and has only been clearly documented in a specific strain known as the Andes virus in South America [26]. Figure 2: Mode of Hantavirus transmission to humans. PATHOGENESIS After the virus has entered the body via the respiratory system, it focuses on endothelial cells that line blood vessels, specifically in the lungs and kidneys. The cells are not killed directly by the virus but by the body's own immune response (cytokine storm) that goes out of control, leading to increased vascular permeability and leakage of fluid [27]. The diseases are mainly two, according to the viral strain and geographical location: 1- Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) "Old World" (Europe and Asia): It starts with fever, headache, and back pain. Later, hypotension, bleeding, and acute kidney failure develop. 2- Hanta Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) "New World" (Americas): flu-like symptoms at the onset that rapidly progresses (within days) to acute respiratory failure as a result of fluid in the alveoli, leading to cardiogenic shock and severe hypoxia [28]. PREVENTION AND CONTROL In general, environmentally sound practices must be adopted to prevent transmission between humans and rodent vectors within the surrounding environment [29]. Undoubtedly, proper preventive measures remain the first and last line of defense (Figure 3). Here are three important preventative measures: 1- Rodent control can be achieved through various methods, especially by eliminating rodent-proof living areas, whether in homes or workplaces, and by cleaning the surrounding environment of debris and waste to prevent rodent hiding places [30]. 2- Safe cleaning of contaminated areas is critical step to avoid inhaling the virus. Ventilation is essential before cleaning begins, and the area should be sprayed with a household disinfectant solution (chlorine(, according to the recommended instructions. It is advisable to wear rubber or plastic gloves and a strong mask. After cleaning, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after removing the gloves [31] . 3- Community awareness and vulnerable individuals especially farmers, sanitation workers, and hunters in the wild [32]. Hantavirus: A Zoonotic Pathogen and Its Role in Achieving Sustainable Development 615 Volume 03 Issue 07 July 2026 Corresponding Author: Ozdan Akram Ghareeb Figure 3: Preventing Hantavirus infection: A Guide to safety. The One Health Approach At the core of this ecosystem lies the One Health triad, this virus cannot be addressed through medicine alone since its survival depends on three interconnected pillars: • Human Health: Lung and kidney vulnerabilities to the virus. • Animal Health: Rodents harboring and chronically disseminating the pathogen. • Environmental Health: Ecosystems and climate conditions that govern rodent habitats [33,34]. The link between combating Hantavirus and achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals is deeply rooted in the One Health approach [35]. Controlling a zoonotic infection requires more than just hospitals; it necessitates comprehensive improvements in society, the economy, and the environment. On the other hand the relationship between controlling Hantavirus and achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is deeply rooted in the "One Health" approach. This concept recognizes that human health, animal health, and environmental health are all intrinsically connected [36]. Here is a breakdown of how managing Hantavirus directly supports specific SDGs (Figure 4): 1. Core Concept: The One Health Synergy The circles that intersect are Human Health, Animal Health (rodents), and Environmental Health (forests/water). The virus in the environment and animal populations is stopped so it never gets a chance to spillover into humans by dealing with its root causes [37]. 2. Direct Health & Economic Impacts • SDG 3: Good Health & Well-Being The Link: Better disease tracking, spotting cases earlier, and getting the public to understand things like not breathing in dust from rodent droppings can cut how many people get Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and die from those diseases. The Goal: Strengthening global health systems and reducing the number of deaths that can be prevented [38]. • SDG 8: Decent Work & Economic Growth The Link: People suffering from long-term or chronic illnesses such as HPS or HFRS are taken out of work either temporarily or permanently. In this case, by preventing the diseases, the community will have a healthier and more productive workforce. The Goal: Mitigating the economic impact of disease on local economies and sustaining labor participation [39]. • SDG 1: No Poverty The Link: In many parts of the world, a severe medical situation can lead to unplayable medical bills or take away the main earner for a household. The Goal: Protecting at-risk groups from health-related poverty by preventing crippling illnesses that can lead to financial ruin [40]. 3. Infrastructure & Environmental Management • SDG 11: Sustainable Cities & Communities The Link: Urban and rural planning is a big part of virus control. Good waste management, building structures that keep out rodents, and overall cleanliness lower human-rodent contact. The Goal: Safe, disease-resistant housing and urban environments [41]. Hantavirus: A Zoonotic Pathogen and Its Role in Achieving Sustainable Development 616 Volume 03 Issue 07 July 2026 Corresponding Author: Ozdan Akram Ghareeb • SDG 15: Life on Land The Link: An ecosystem that is healthy and in balance will be able to manage itself naturally. Therefore, support for the maintenance of natural habitats would automatically result in the presence of rodents' natural predators, such as owls, hawks, and foxes, to keep their population in check. The Goal: Promoting biodiversity and managing ecological habitats to prevent a significant rise in carrier rodents [42]. SDG 13: Climate Action The Link: Unseasonal weather creates unbalances in the ecosystem. For example, heavy rainfall followed by a period of drought can lead to massive booms in food supplies for rodents. This in turn leads to population explosions among rodents - and subsequent spikes in human Hantavirus cases. The Goal is to predict these climate-induced ecological changes and build environmental resistance in order to be able to forecast and control zoonotic disease outbreaks [43]. Figure 4: Linking Hantavirus Infection to Achieving Sustainable Development. CONCLUSION This will enable us to build a more sustainable and resilient world in multiple development fronts by taking a holistic approach to Hantavirus in terms of ecology, urban sanitation, climate tracking, and healthcare. Such viewing of Hantavirus, not just as a medical crisis but as an environmental and systemic challenge, will help the global health initiatives to hit multiple developmental goals at the same time. papers.title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses circulate in an ecological web linking rodent population dynamics, contaminated environmental substrates and the accidental human host, causing two severe syndromes for which no licensed antiviral therapy exists [15,22]. We formulate and rigorously analyse a coupled SEIR-SEIV model joining a rodent reservoir with chronic lifelong shedding and no recovery, an environmental viral compartment V accumulating shed material, and a dead-end human SEIR population. For the deterministic system we establish well-posedness and derive, by the next-generation method [39], a basic reproduction number that decomposes additively, R 0 = R dir 0 + R 0 ind , separating the direct rodent-to-rodent route from the indirect environmental one. We prove that R 0 is the exact threshold, the disease-free and endemic equilibria being globally asymptotically stable for R 0 ≤ 1 and R 0 > 1 respectively, through Volterra-type Lyapunov functions. Under multiplicative Brownian noise on (S R , E R , I R , V ) the system remains globally positive. We show that the classical Itô-corrected threshold R s < R 0 , standard in this literature, is necessary but not sucient for extinction once more than one infected compartment is present its usual derivation counts the Itô correction twice and we exhibit an explicit counterexample. We replace it by a variational exponent Λ, computable by nested one-dimensional bisection, that bounds the top Lyapunov exponent of the infected block: Λ < 0 forces global almost-sure exponential extinction even when R 0 > 1. Under small noise the solution stays within an O( ∑ i σ i 2 ) mean-square deviation of the endemic equilibrium up to its exit time; the criterion is one-sided, since persistence is documented numerically but not proved. Forcing the environmental decay rate with the observed temperature cycle of Shaanxi Province (China) reproduces the documented winter peak of HFRS incidence. As the forced system is nonautonomous, we compute its periodic reproduction number by Floquet analysis and obtain R per 0 ≈ 2.15 against R 0 = 1.63. A complementary rainfall forcing with a one-year lag captures the interannual peaks (20052016), while the residual uctuations, explained by neither driver, provide an empirical rationale for the stochastic framework.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

source_records.title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir
source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses circulate in an ecological web linking rodent population dynamics, contaminated environmental substrates and the accidental human host, causing two severe syndromes for which no licensed antiviral therapy exists [15,22]. We formulate and rigorously analyse a coupled SEIR-SEIV model joining a rodent reservoir with chronic lifelong shedding and no recovery, an environmental viral compartment V accumulating shed material, and a dead-end human SEIR population. For the deterministic system we establish well-posedness and derive, by the next-generation method [39], a basic reproduction number that decomposes additively, R 0 = R dir 0 + R 0 ind , separating the direct rodent-to-rodent route from the indirect environmental one. We prove that R 0 is the exact threshold, the disease-free and endemic equilibria being globally asymptotically stable for R 0 ≤ 1 and R 0 > 1 respectively, through Volterra-type Lyapunov functions. Under multiplicative Brownian noise on (S R , E R , I R , V ) the system remains globally positive. We show that the classical Itô-corrected threshold R s < R 0 , standard in this literature, is necessary but not sucient for extinction once more than one infected compartment is present its usual derivation counts the Itô correction twice and we exhibit an explicit counterexample. We replace it by a variational exponent Λ, computable by nested one-dimensional bisection, that bounds the top Lyapunov exponent of the infected block: Λ < 0 forces global almost-sure exponential extinction even when R 0 > 1. Under small noise the solution stays within an O( ∑ i σ i 2 ) mean-square deviation of the endemic equilibrium up to its exit time; the criterion is one-sided, since persistence is documented numerically but not proved. Forcing the environmental decay rate with the observed temperature cycle of Shaanxi Province (China) reproduces the documented winter peak of HFRS incidence. As the forced system is nonautonomous, we compute its periodic reproduction number by Floquet analysis and obtain R per 0 ≈ 2.15 against R 0 = 1.63. A complementary rainfall forcing with a one-year lag captures the interannual peaks (20052016), while the residual uctuations, explained by neither driver, provide an empirical rationale for the stochastic framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environments and humans, causing severe disease with no licensed antivirals. Methods: A coupled SEIR‑SEIV model links a rodent reservoir with chronic shedding, an environmental viral compartment, and a dead‑end human SEIR population. Results: The basic reproduction number R0 = R_dir0 + R_ind0 separates direct and environmental transmission; R0 is the exact threshold with globally stable disease‑free and endemic equilibria; the stochastic system stays positive under Brownian noise; the usual Ito‑corrected threshold Rs < R0 is insufficient; a variational exponent Λ (<0) ensures almost‑sure extinction; small noise keeps solutions within O(∑σ_i^2) of the endemic equilibrium; temperature forcing reproduces winter HFRS peaks (periodic R ≈2.15 vs R0=1.63) and rainfall forcing captures interannual peaks 2005‑2016. Contribution: Provides rigorous threshold and stability theory, a new stochastic extinction criterion, and demonstrates environmental drivers of hantavirus incidence. Limitations: Persistence is only shown numerically, not analytically, and the work is limited to abstract‑level description without empirical validation.

papers.title_zh: 一种带环境储存库的随机汉坦病毒模型

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 在一个生态网络中循环,连接啮齿动物种群动态、受污染的环境基质和偶然的人类宿主,导致两种严重综合征,且目前没有获批的抗病毒疗法。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建并严格分析了一个耦合的 SEIR‐SEIV 模型,将具有慢性终身排病毒的啮齿动物储库、环境病毒室 V,以及无后续传播的人类 SEIR 群体相结合。
analysis_zh.results: 他们推导出基本再生数 R0 = R_dir0 + R_ind0,将直接啮齿动物间传播和间接环境途径分离,证明 R0 是精确阈值,且无病平衡和流行平衡在全局上渐近稳定,展示在乘性布朗噪声下随机系统保持全局正性,证明常用的 Ito 校正阈值 Rs < R0 不足,提出变分指数 Λ(Λ<0 强制几乎必然灭绝),发现小噪声使解保持在 O(∑σ_i^2) 的流行平衡邻域内,并且温度强迫能够再现记录的冬季肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 峰值,其周期性再生数约为 2.15,而 R0 = 1.63;降雨强迫则捕捉到 2005‐2016 年的年际峰值。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作为 汉坦病毒 模型提供了严格的阈值理论和全局稳定性证明,提出了新的随机灭绝准则 (Λ),并将环境驱动因素与观测到的发病模式关联,推动了对 汉坦病毒 传播的理论和生态认识。
analysis_zh.limitations: 持久性仅通过数值方式记录,未给出解析证明;论文仅提供摘要,未报告除所述强迫外的实证验证。

papers.title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with a hemorrhagic syndrome and the development of renal failure. It belongs to the group of severe and potentially life-threatening pathologies in children, both worldwide and in Ukraine in particular. Rodents serve as reservoirs and carriers of infection, while hantaviruses are the causative agents. In the Americas, they cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, whereas in Europe, they lead to hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or its milder form - epidemic nephropathy. Aim - to demonstrate the stages and challenges of diagnosing hantavirus infection through a clinical case in a child. Clinical case. This case describes the course of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in a 14-year-old child residing in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. The case highlights hantavirus infection as a disease that may mimic other diagnoses. The diagnosis of hantavirus infection presenting with hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure, particularly in the pediatric population, is complicated due to its rarity and similarity of symptoms to other inflammatory diseases. Conclusions. Hantavirus infection should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with fever, signs of renal failure, hemorrhagic manifestations, and thrombocytopenia, regardless of age or region of residence. The specific diagnostic methods include the detection of IgM and IgG antibodies to hantavirus using ELISA and immunoblotting. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was obtained from the child's parents to participate in the study. The authors declare no conflict of interest.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒感染儿童病例:诊断挑战与临床报告

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒感染是一种罕见的人畜共患疾病,可导致出血综合征和肾功能衰竭,对全球及乌克兰的儿童构成严重威胁。

papers.title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for two severe human diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40%. Although single-layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies have advanced our understanding of hantavirus biology, true multi-omics integration remains scarce, leaving systems-level mechanisms of disease severity and host–pathogen interactions unresolved. High-throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus–host interactions. This review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI-enabled approaches in hantavirus research. Genomic studies have clarified viral diversity, evolution, and reassortment, while transcriptomics has identified regulatory networks governing endothelial and innate immune responses. Proteomics has revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation, endothelial dysfunction, and potential therapeutic targeting, whereas metabolomics indicates substantial metabolic reprogramming during infection, although dedicated studies remain limited. AI-based approaches are increasingly applied to outbreak prediction, surveillance, and risk modeling. Drawing on successful multi-omics frameworks developed for other viral infections, we discuss opportunities to improve biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and future precision medicine strategies for hantavirus infections.

papers.title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). In Europe, Puumala virus and Dobrava virus account for most recognised disease; Seoul virus is relevant to ports and urban settings. The 2026 MV Hondius cruise-ship cluster of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infections, involving passengers from 23 countries, has highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease. OBJECTIVES: To review hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, and clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness in Europe, with emphasis on endemic Puumala virus (PUUV), Dobrava virus (DOBV), and Seoul virus (SEOV), and to clarify the separate relevance of imported Andes virus (ANDV) infection for travel medicine and maritime response. SOURCES: We conducted a structured narrative review of literature published from January 2000 to May 2026, prioritising surveillance reports, systematic and narrative reviews, rodent ecology studies, diagnostic evaluations, external quality assessment studies, and outbreak investigations. WHO, ECDC, and International Health Regulations guidance documents were also reviewed. CONTENT: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and shaped by reservoir ecology, biome-specific rodent dynamics, clinical awareness, diagnostic capacity, and surveillance practice. Climate effects are indirect and regionally variable, mediated by mast years, predator-prey dynamics, winter conditions, land use, reservoir density, and human exposure. Diagnostic preparedness is uneven, particularly for molecular detection. Imported ANDV infection is rare in Europe but relevant to travel medicine and high-consequence preparedness because it can cause severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and, unlike endemic European hantaviruses, has documented person-to-person transmission. IMPLICATIONS: European preparedness should prioritise PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV through rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early warning.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, motivating a review of European risk and preparedness.
analysis.main_directions: The review addresses endemic Puumala, Dobrava, and Seoul viruses and imported Andes virus, focusing on epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness.
analysis.current_state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and driven by reservoir ecology and climate‑mediated rodent dynamics, while diagnostic capacity, especially molecular testing, remains uneven.
analysis.gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship Andes virus cluster exposed urgent gaps in surveillance harmonisation, molecular diagnostics, and overall preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease.
analysis.future_research: Recommendations call for rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing HFRS and HCPS, prompting a review of European risk and preparedness. Main directions: The review examines endemic PUUV, DOBV, SEOV and imported ANDV, covering epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness. Current state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, shaped by reservoir ecology and climate‑mediated rodent dynamics, while diagnostic capacity, especially molecular testing, is uneven. Gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship ANDV outbreak highlighted urgent gaps in surveillance harmonisation, molecular diagnostics, and overall preparedness for endemic and imported infections. Future research: Prioritise rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, enhanced molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 在气候变化和全球流动时代的欧洲风险与防备。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性疾病,导致肾综合征出血热和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,促使对欧洲风险和防备进行审查。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述涉及地方性普马拉病毒、Dobrava 病毒和 首尔病毒es 以及输入性 安第斯病毒,重点关注流行病学、生态学、临床识别、诊断和防备。
analysis_zh.current_state: 欧洲 汉坦病毒 流行病学呈异质性,由宿主生态和气候驱动的啮齿动物动态所决定,同时诊断能力,尤其是分子检测,仍然不均衡。
analysis_zh.gaps: 2026 年邮轮 安第斯病毒 集群暴露出在监测统一、分子诊断以及对地方性和输入性 汉坦病毒 疾病整体防备方面的紧迫缺口。
analysis_zh.future_research: 建议呼吁进行啮齿动物生物监测、统一监测、改进分子诊断以及本地校准的早期预警系统。

papers.title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi-country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in 2026. To investigate the origin and evolutionary history of the virus responsible for the outbreak, we analyzed complete ANDV small (S), medium (M), and large (L) genome segment sequences from Chile alongside outbreak-associated and publicly available genome sequences. Across all three segment-specific phylogenies, the outbreak virus clustered within an ANDV Clade III cluster spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia in Argentina and were most closely related to a human-derived ANDV (p1236) collected in Los Rios Region of Chile in 2012, representing the closest known historical relative of the outbreak-associated virus. Phylogeographic analysis showed that the genetically distinct ANDV Clade V lineage circulating in central Chile was not closely related to the cruise ship outbreak-associated genomes, thereby reducing the likelihood that the index cases acquired infection through zoonotic spillover while traveling through the Maule Region. These findings trace the geographic origin of the outbreak-associated virus to a defined corridor, the Hua Hum Pass, a cross-border zone connecting Neuquen Province in Argentina with the Los Rios and La Araucania Regions of Chile.

Across all three segment-specific phylogenies, the outbreak virus clustered within an ANDV Clade III cluster spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia in Argentina and were most closely related to a human-derived ANDV (p1236) collected in Los Rios Region of Chile in 2012, representing the closest known historical relative of the outbreak-associated virus. Phylogeographic analysis showed that the genetically distinct ANDV Clade V lineage circulating in central Chile was not closely related to the cruise ship outbreak-associated genomes, thereby reducing the likelihood that the index cases acquired infection through zoonotic spillover while traveling through the Maule Region. These findings trace the geographic origin of the outbreak-associated virus to a defined corridor, the Hua Hum Pass, a cross-border zone connecting Neuquen Province in Argentina with the Los Rios and La Araucania Regions of Chile.

papers.title_zh: 历史性跨境 安第斯病毒 系统揭示了邮轮 汉坦病毒肺综合征 爆发的起源

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)在2026年导致了在邮轮乘客和船员中出现的多国汉坦病毒肺综合征爆发,凸显了跨境公共卫生威胁。
analysis_zh.methods: 对来自智利的完整安第斯病毒小(S)、中(M)和大(L)基因组片段序列进行分析,并结合与暴发相关的以及公开可得的基因组序列一起分析。
analysis_zh.results: 三段基因的系统发育树将本次暴发病毒定位于安第斯病毒III类群,覆盖智利南部和巴塔哥尼亚北部,并确定其与2012年来源于智利洛斯里奥斯的人的分离株(p1236)最为相近;系统地理分析显示,位于智利中部的独特V类群并无关联,降低了在马乌莱地区跨种传播的可能性;地理来源被追溯至连接阿根廷内乌肯省与智利洛斯里奥斯及拉阿劳卡尼亚的华胡姆通道走廊。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究阐明了邮轮暴发的进化谱系和地理来源,为跨境汉坦病毒传播的监测与控制措施提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息;样本量、详细方法、定量结果以及更广泛的流行病学背景均未报告。

papers.title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate t-PAIC concentration changes across severity levels in HFRS patients and evaluate its value in predicting disease severity, providing a potential biomarker for HFRS severity assessment and monitoring. METHODS: t-PAIC levels were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls. Routine laboratory tests assessed WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, and PT. HFRS-specific antibodies were detected using the colloidal gold method. Spearman correlation analysis evaluated associations between t-PAIC and clinical indices. Ordinal logistic regression identified risk factors linked to disease severity. ROC curve analysis assessed the predictive performance of t-PAIC for HFRS severity. RESULTS: t-PAIC levels progressively increased with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients. t-PAIC showed significant positive correlations with leukocyte count (r = 0.6082; p < 0.01), Cr (r = 0.3567; p < 0.01), urea (r = 0.4376; p < 0.01), UA (r = 0.3201; p < 0.01), APTT (r = 0.6182; p < 0.01), and PT (r = 0.2997; p < 0.01), and significant inverse correlations with PLT (r = -0.6177; p < 0.01), HDL (r = -0.3074; p < 0.01), and ALB (r = -0.4790; p < 0.01). ROC analysis revealed t-PAIC had good predictive value for disease severity (AUC = 0.796, 95% CI: 0.724-0.867, p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: t-PAIC levels closely reflect HFRS severity and associated clinical features, including renal dysfunction and coagulation abnormalities, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

analysis.background: The study addresses the need for biomarkers to assess severity in hantaan virus‑induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS).
analysis.methods: t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex (t‑PAIC) concentrations were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; routine laboratory indices and HFRS‑specific antibodies were also obtained, and statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve assessment.
analysis.results: t‑PAIC levels rose progressively with disease severity, peaking in critically ill patients; t‑PAIC correlated positively with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), creatinine (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), uric acid (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997) and inversely with platelet count (r=-0.6177), HDL (r=-0.3074), and albumin (r=-0.4790) (all p<0.01); ROC analysis gave AUC=0.796 (95% CI 0.724‑0.867, p<0.001) for predicting severity.
analysis.contribution: The findings suggest t‑PAIC may serve as a useful biomarker for monitoring HFRS severity and associated renal and coagulation disturbances.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed methodological and cohort information, as well as any authors‑stated limitations, are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study seeks biomarkers for hantaan virus‑induced HFRS severity. Methods: t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 patients and 37 controls, with routine labs, antibody testing, Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC analysis performed. Results: t‑PAIC increased with severity, showed strong positive correlations with leukocytes, creatinine, urea, uric acid, APTT, PT and negative correlations with platelets, HDL, albumin (all p<0.01); ROC AUC=0.796 for severity prediction. Contribution: t‑PAIC appears a promising biomarker for HFRS severity and related renal/coagulation changes. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed methods, sample characteristics, and explicit limitations are not reported.

analysis_zh.background: 本研究针对评估汉滩病毒诱导的肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)严重程度所需的生物标志物。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过化学发光免疫测定法测定156例肾综合征出血热患者和37例健康对照的t‐PA/PAI‐1复合物(t‐PAIC)浓度;同时获取常规实验室指标和肾综合征出血热特异性抗体,并进行Spearman相关、序数逻辑回归和ROC曲线评估等统计分析。
analysis_zh.results: t‐PAIC水平随疾病严重程度逐步升高,在危重症患者中达到峰值;t‐PAIC与白细胞计数(r=0.6082)、肌酐(r=0.3567)、尿素(r=0.4376)、尿酸(r=0.3201)、APTT(r=0.6182)、PT(r=0.2997)呈正相关,且与血小板计数(r=-0.6177)、高密度脂蛋白(r=-0.3074)和白蛋白(r=-0.4790)呈负相关(均p<0.01);ROC分析预测严重程度的AUC为0.796(95% CI 0.724‐0.867,p<0.001)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 结果表明t‐PAIC可作为监测肾综合征出血热严重程度及相关肾脏和凝血功能障碍的有用生物标志物。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细的方法学和队列信息,也未包含作者所述的任何局限性。
